resources.string: Medial cutaway
Medial view of one cerebral hemisphere, with the front at left. A small cutaway in the frontal lobe reveals white matter beneath the cortex.
Cerebral cortex
Cortical gray matter forms the folded outer layer of the hemisphere. Its ridges are gyri, and the grooves between them are sulci.
Subcortical white matter
Beneath the cortex, bundles of axons connect different regions of the same hemisphere, the opposite hemisphere, and deeper structures.
Corpus callosum
This curved bundle of white matter crosses the midline to connect the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
Cingulate gyrus
This fold of cortex follows the upper curve of the corpus callosum. The cingulate sulcus lies just above it.
Parieto-occipital sulcus
This deep groove marks the boundary between the parietal and occipital lobes on the medial surface.
Nerve cutaway
A peripheral nerve trunk opened along its length and across its end. One fascicle is shown with individual fibers exposed.
Epineurium
This outer connective tissue encloses the whole nerve and extends between its fascicles.
Nerve fascicle
A fascicle is a bundle of nerve fibers that runs lengthwise within the nerve.
Perineurium
This layered sheath encloses a single fascicle, not the entire nerve.
Endoneurium
This delicate connective tissue surrounds individual nerve fibers within a fascicle. It lies outside the Schwann cells associated with the axons.
Roots and rami
One side of a spinal cord segment, with the back at the top. The two roots meet in a short spinal nerve, which then divides into two primary branches, or rami.
Dorsal root
Sensory fibers enter the back of the spinal cord through this root. Their neuron cell bodies lie in the swelling along it, the dorsal root ganglion.
Ventral root
Motor fibers leave the front of the spinal cord through this root. It has no ganglion and joins the dorsal root beyond the dorsal root ganglion.
Mixed spinal nerve
Where the two roots unite, their sensory and motor fibers run together in a short trunk before it branches.
Dorsal ramus
This smaller mixed branch supplies deep back muscles and carries sensation from skin over the back.
Ventral ramus
This larger mixed branch carries fibers to and from the front and sides of the trunk and, at limb levels, to and from the limbs.
Sensory ganglion
A dorsal root ganglion opened lengthwise, with the spinal cord side at left and the spinal nerve side at right. This is one example of a sensory ganglion.
Connective tissue capsule
A connective tissue coat surrounds the ganglion and continues along the dorsal root at its ends.
Sensory neuron cell body
Most of these large, round cell bodies lie near the outer part of the ganglion. Satellite glial cells form a thin coat around each cell body.
Sensory fiber bundles
Bundles of sensory axons pass mainly through the center of the ganglion and continue toward the spinal cord on one side and the spinal nerve on the other.
T-shaped sensory axon
A single process leaves the cell body and divides into two branches. One extends to the periphery, and the other enters the spinal cord. The sensory signal does not need a synapse in the ganglion.
